2. It is stated in the petition that the petitioner, Prof. Golam Azam, is a Bangladeshi citizen by birth having been born at Dhaka on the 22nd November, 1922; that his father late Moulana Ghulam Kabir was born in village Birgram, Police Station Nabinagar, District Comilla now Brahmanbaria and from generations they are permanent residents in the terriories now comprised in Bangladesh; that the petitioner passed the Intermediate Examination from the Islamia Intermediate Government College, Dhaka and then obtained his Graduation and his Masters Degree in Political Science from the University of Dhaka; that the petitioner was General Secretary of the Student's Union of the then Fazlul Huq Muslim Hall and he was also General Secretary of the Dhaka University Students Union wherein he played a very vital role in the Bengali Language Movement and as the General Secretary of the Dhaka University Students Union; the petitioner read a memorandum before the then Prime Minister of Pakistan on the 27th of November, 1948 at the Gymnasium ground of the Dhaka University urging him to make Bengali as one of the State Languages, as one of the main demands; that the petitioner was a professor of Political Science for five years in the Carmichael College, Rangpur; that he fought for restoration of democracy during the Ayub regime and was General Secretary of the Eastern Wing of the Pakistan Democratic Movement (PDM); that because of his active role in various democratic movements the petitioner was arrested once in 1955, then in 1964 but he was released by the order of the Dhaka High Court on Habeas Corpus petition; that the petitioner dedicated his life for the establishment of Islamic Social Justice in all spheres of the society and he became the Ameer (President) of the Jamaat-e-Islami of the then East Pakistan in 1969; that in the General Election of 1970 Jamaat-e-Islami took part in the election and obtained the second highest votes, next to the Awami League in the then East Pakistan; that from the election of 1970 political rivalry and enmity developed between the Jamaat-e-Islami and the Awami League and the petitioner being the head of the Jamaat-e-Islami became the target of the Awami League, which later on, formed the first Government in the independent Bangladesh; that in spite of political differences with Awami League the petitioner advocated for transfer of power to the Awami League as it obtained the highest number of seats in the then National Assembly; that during the liberation struggle the petitioner was actively engaged in helping people and saving them from the military atrocities of Yahya regime, but even then the Awami League considered the petitioner their arch enemy; that the petitioner was a resident of Bangladesh on the 25th of March, 1971 and he continued to be so resident and on the 22nd of November, 1971 he went to Lahore for attending his party's central working committee meeting and on the 3rd of December, 1971 the petitioner was returning to Dhaka by plane but the plane could not land at Dhaka Airport because of the war and as such the plane at first landed at Colombo and as there was bombing at that time at Karachi Airport the plane went to Jeddah where the petitioner remained a few days wherefrom he was sent back to Karachi along with the other passengers; that the petitioner had to remain in Pakistan against his will for some months as the then Government of Pakistan did not allow any Bangladeshi citizen to leave Pakistan, that the petitioner tried to go to London in the month of March, 1972 for making contact with his family but failed to obtain any travel document in Pakistan and thereafter arranged a Pakistani passport to go to Hajj in the month of December, 1972; that the petitioner during the Hajj met friends & acquaintances from Bangladesh who went for Hajj who informed him about a political mis-propaganda against the petitioner in Bangladesh; that thereafter the petitioner went to London in the first week of April, 1973 where he came to learn from a news item published in the Bangladesh Observer to the effect that he along with 38 others were declared by a notification dated 18.4.73 of the Department of Home Affairs of Bangladesh to be disqualified to become citizen of Bangladesh. 

 3. It is also stated in the petition that the petitioner found it impossible to return to Bangladesh and he stayed in England against his will but 1ie never went to Pakistan nor he obtained nationality or citizenship of any other country; that after the publication of the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 the petitioner continued to reside in England since the first week of April, 1973; that in the meantime in 1975 there was a change of Government and the political situation in Bangladesh; and the new Government of Bangladesh by a notification dated 17.1.76 (Annexure-C) invited applications from those persons whose citizenship was cancelled by the previous Government for restoration of their citizenship and accordingly the petitioner sent an application on 20.5.76 to the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Bangladesh praying for restoration of his citizenship but having received no reply the petitioner sent another application on 12.1.77 to the Chief Martial Law Administrator renewing his prayer for restoration of citizenship but the petitioner received a reply from the Ministry of Home Affairs dated 23.4.77 (Annexure-E) to the following effect: 

 4. The petitioner also received a letter dated 29.9.77 from the office of the High Commissioner for Bangladesh in England (Annexure-E 1) to the same effect; that in the meantime the petitioner lost his father in 1973 and his old mother applied on 14.11.77 to the Government of Bangladesh praying for restoration of the citizenship to the petitioner which was refused but the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh by their letter dated 11.3.78 expressed their no objection for granting visa to the petitioner to see his ailing mother and accordingly the petitioner obtained visa from London and entered Bangladesh on 11.7.78 with a visa for three months; that after his arrival in Bangladesh on 11.7.78 the petitioner was registered by the concerned authority as a Foreigner; that the petitioner obtained extension of his visa twice and then in order to avoid possible ouster from the court he filed an application for registration as a citizen of Bangladesh to the Ministry of Home Affairs on 8.11.78 surrendering his Pakistani passport to the authority concerned, that thereafter the petitioner has been permanently residing in Bangladesh considering himself a citizen of Bangladesh by birth; that on 27.5.80 some members of the Parliament inquired from the Government about the stay of the petitioner in Bangladesh on which the then Minister for Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh made a statement in the Parliament to the effect that the petitioner had filed an application praying for registration as a citizen of Bangladesh by surrendering his Pakistani passport and that the matter is pending decision of the Government; that thereafter the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration Section vide letter dated 28.4.81 asked the petitioner to submit an affidavit with oath of allegiance to Bangladesh and the petitioner submitted the required affidavit on 30.4.81; that after a long silence the petitioner received a letter dated 3.12.86 from the Ministry of Home Affairs (Annexure H-1) requesting him to let the Ministry to know as to why he was staying in Bangladesh without visa since he had not approached the authority for extension of visa after he had registered his name with the Foreigners Registration Office on 12.7.78 to which the petitioner sent a reply on 22.12.86 (Annexure H-2) asserting himself as a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and informing that on 8.11.78 he made an application for restoration of his citizenship by surrendering his passport and that his application was under the active consideration of the authorities; that the petitioner also asserted himself as a citizen of Bangladesh in a Press Conference held on 30.5.88; that the name of the petitioner was also published in the voter list published on 5.8.83 (Annexure-M) as well as in the voter list published on 15.2.90 (Annexure-I); that the petitioner thought that the clouds about his citizenship was over and he was a citizen of Bangladesh; that the petitioner was elected as the Chief of his party, Jamaat-e-Islami of Bangladesh, and after the general election held in 1991 the Prime Minister personally met the petitioner for the support of his party before formation of the Government and during the election of the President both the candidates for the office of President of the country also requested him for the support of his party; that all an a sudden the petitioner received a notice dated 23.3.92 (Annexure-K) from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Immigration Branch to show cause by 10 AM of 24th of March, 1992 why the petitioner should not be deported from Bangladesh and why other legal actions should not be taken against him as he had been disqualified to be the citizen of Bangladesh by a Notification dated 18.4.73 and he is a registered Foreigner and as he became the Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami, Bangladesh in contravention of Article 38 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, to which the petitioner gave a reply on 24.3.92 (Annexure K-1) asserting his right as a citizen of Bangladesh and denying the allegations made in the show cause notice and also soliciting for personal hearing in the matter; but the respondent No. 1 illegally arrested the petitioner and detained him at the Dhaka Central Jail by issuing an order of detention dated 24.3.92 under section 3 of the Foreigners Act, 1946; that the petitioner sent a demand for justice notice to the respondent No.1 (Annexure-L) and thereafter challenged the order of detention by filing Writ Petition No. 1148 of 1992 on which a Rule was issued on 30.3.92. 

 6. The respondent No. 1 controverted the statements of the petitioner made in the petition by filing an affidavit-in-opposition wherein it is stated that the petitioner and his fore-fathers were born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh but he is "now" not a citizen of Bangladesh as he has been staying abroad since before the liberation of Bangladesh; that the petitioner had actively participated in the anti-Bangladeshi campaign both inside and outside the country during the war of liberation and he continued to be a citizen of Pakistan that Armed Cadre of Jamaat-e-Islami such as Rajaker, Al-Badr and Al-Shams were placed under the disposal of Pakistan Army in the then East Pakistan during the war of liberation; that as the petitioner had actively participated in the Anti-liberation Movement the Government of Bangladesh disqualified him from being a citizen of Bangladesh by the impugned Notification (Annexure-B); that the people of Bangladesh are well aware about the role of the petitioner during the war of liberation who actively collaborated with Pakistani Army in raising the Rajakers, Al-Badr and Al-Shams, that the conduct of the petitioner makes it clear that he placed the Jamaat-e-Islami at the disposal of Pakistan Army; that it was not true that the petitioner was staying in Pakistan against his will, that it was also not true that the petitioner went to Saudi Arabia in 1972 for the purpose of performing Hajj but his mission to Saudi Arabia was to orchestrate anti-Bangladesh sentiment and he lobbied actively to dissuade the Muslim countries from recognizing Bangladesh as an independent state; that in the year 1972 the petitioner had organized "East Pakistan Recovery Committee" in Lahore; that in the same year the petitioner attended the Islamic Youth Conference in Riadh wherein he appealed to all of them to join in liberation struggle for recapturing East Pakistan and he had also organized a committee for recapturing East Pakistan in London; that in 1973 the petitioner went to Bengali in Libya to attend the conference of the Foreign Ministers of the Islamic countries and there he made an appeal not to recognize Bangladesh as an independent State; that the petitioner met the Saudi Badsha for seven times from 1973 to 1976 for not giving recognition to Bangladesh; that the Government being satisfied about the conduct of the petitioner passed the impugned order (Annexure-B); that during his stay in the United Kingdom after the liberation of Bangladesh he did not endeavor to obtain citizenship of Bangladesh and for his conduct and continuous citizenship of Pakistan he was declared not to be citizen of Bangladesh by the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette on 22.6.73; that the petitioner went abroad before the liberation of Bangladesh and he did not submit his oath of allegiance to Bangladesh as he continued to be the citizen of Pakistan; that immediately after the liberation of Bangladesh as many as 14187 persons living in the United Kingdom obtained Bangladeshi Passport by surrendering their Pakistani Passport but the petitioner did not make any attempt to obtain Bangladeshi Passport and he remained as a Pakistani citizen in London; that the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 disqualifying the petitioner and 38 persons from being citizen of Bangladesh was issued in accordance with the provision of Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972; that the petitioner was permitted to travel to Bangladesh as a foreign national to see his ailing mother after his prayer for citizenship of Bangladesh was turned down twice by the Government; that the entry of the petitioner in Bangladesh was admittedly as a Pakistani citizen and he continued to stay in Bangladesh as a registered foreign national; that the petitioner came to Bangladesh with Pakistani Passport which was issued by Pakistan Embassy in London on 11.1.77, that the petitioner applied to the Government of Pakistan for his Passport affirming that he was a Pakistani National and he obtained extension of his visa twice in Bangladesh as a Pakistani national and thereby admitted himself to be a Pakistani national even in the year 1978, that the petitioner applied to the Ministry of Home Affairs for Bangladeshi citizenship and his application for Citizenship of Bangladesh was not supported by oath of allegiance as required by law; that the petitioner cannot be considered as a Bangladeshi Citizen as he had been staying in Bangladesh after registering himself as a Foreign national on his arrival with a Pakistani Passport; that the petitioner did not submit oath of allegiance voluntarily when he applied for restoration of citizenship of Bangladesh but on the asking of the Government he submitted his oath of allegiance on 30.4.81, that the petitioner was staying in Bangladesh illegally without extending his visa for which he was asked to show cause in 1986 and that non-consideration of his application for citizenship for a long time would not entitle the petitioner to be a citizen of Bangladesh. 

 7. It is also stated in the affidavit-in- opposition that the petitioner knew very well that he was residing in Bangladesh as a foreign national by registering himself as a foreign national and he had only applied for his citizenship and as such his enrollment as a voter was a bonafide mistake due to concealment of facts about his foreign nationality; that the selection of the petitioner as Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami of Bangladesh was illegal, he being a foreign national and he became the head of the political party to destabilise the sovereignty of Bangladesh; that the fact that the Presidential Candidate went to the petitioner for his support would not ipso facto entitle the petitioner to be a citizen of Bangladesh; that the petitioner by his conduct had renounced his citizenship of Bangladesh and thereby he is disqualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh; that the application challenging the impugned notification (Annexure-B) is not tenable in law, rather such a belated application is liable to be rejected; that the petitioner came to Bangladesh with Pakistani Passport and he was registered as a foreign national; that he was disqualified to be a citizen of Bangladesh due to anti-Bangladesh activities and unseeming conduct; that the petitioner's continued stay in Bangladesh as a foreign national without any visa was illegal and that is why he was asked by the Government to explain as to how he was staying in Bangladesh; and as the reasons shown in his reply were not tenable in law, the Government took action under the Foreigners Act 1946 and that the impugned notification Annexure-B was issued neither malafide nor with any political motive or for any collateral purpose. 

 8. In the affidavit-in-reply it is stated that on the 26th of March, 1971 the petitioner became a citizen of Bangladesh by operation of law and continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh; that he had genuine political difference with Awami League, the party which formed the Government in 1972 but he did not participate in the anti-Bangladeshi campaign inside or outside Bangladesh; that it was denied that the petitioner or the Jamaat-e-Islami had any organizational link with Razakar, AI-Shams or Al-Badr, that the domicile of origin of the petitioner being the territories comprised in Bangladesh his position as a citizen of Bangladesh is protected; that the petitioner's case falls in the same category as that of 38 other people who were also disqualified to be citizen of Bangladesh and anyone of them applied for citizenship was readily granted the same; that on the 30th of November, 1973 the then Awami League Government granted a clemency to the persons who were convicted or accused of offences under the Bangladesh Collaborators (Special Tribunal) Order 1972; that the petitioner reiterated the statements made in paragraph 2-12 of the petition and denied the allegation that he played any heinous role during the war of independence. It is also stated that the petitioner could not be held responsible for the alleged rape, arson, looting and genocide, committed by the Pakistan Army. He also denied that during the Hajj in 1972 the petitioner made any anti-Bangladeshi campaign to dissuade the Muslim countries from giving recognition to Bangladesh or that he organised "East Pakistan Recovery Committee" in Lahore in that year or went to Bengazi in Libya for making any appeal to the Foreign Ministers Conference of Islamic Countries not to recognise Bangladesh or the petitioner met the king of Saudi Arabia seven times as alleged. It is also stated therein that under compulsion the petitioner had to retain his Pakistani Passport as a travel document in a foreign country as England. It is also denied that the petitioner entered Bangladesh as a Pakistani citizen and he merely used Pakistani Passport as a travel document; on the other hand, at the earliest opportunity he surrendered his Pakistani Passport to the Bangladesh authority by making fresh application for citizenship; that the petitioner did not enclose his oath of allegiance with the application for citizenship because he was not asked to do so; that it was also denied that the petitioner could not reconcile with the existence of Bangladesh; that it was also denied that the petitioner is a foreign national or he concealed his status for which voter lists were prepared due to bonafide mistake; it is also stated therein that Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 was ultra vires of the Constitution inasmuch it did not provide any guideline to the executive for the exercise of the power under that Article. 

 (i) owes affirms or acknowledges expressly or by conduct allegiance to a foreign state or 

 Provided that citizen of Bangladesh shall not merely by reason of being a citizen or acquiring citizenship of a state specified in or under clause (2) cease to be a citizen of Bangladesh. 

 (2) The Government may grant citizenship of Bangladesh to any person who is a citizen of any state of Europe or North America or of any other state which the Government may by notification in the Official Gazette specify in this behalf. 

 18. In this connection it may be mentioned that the learned Advocate for the petitioner has drawn our attention to section 3 of the Citizenship Act, 1951 and contended that the petitioner acquired the citizenship of Bangladesh by virtue of section 3 but if we go through the provisions of section 3 of the said Act it will appear that those provisions will be of no help in determining the question of citizenship in the present context. It may also be mentioned in this connection that in the petition it has been stated that the petitioner became a citizen of Bangladesh by birth and the learned Advocate for the petitioner has also contended that by virtue of section 4 of the Citizenship Act, 1951 as adopted in Bangladesh by the provisions of PO 48 of 1972 the petitioner acquired citizenship of Bangladesh by birth. But section 4 provides that every person after the commencement of the Act shall be a citizen of Pakistan by birth and there are some exceptions mentioned therein. If we read "Bangladesh" in place of "Pakistan" in section 4 then every person born in Bangladesh after the commencement of this Act shall be citizen of Bangladesh by birth but this Act commenced on or from the 13th of April, 1951 long after the birth of the petitioner. 

 20. This Article provides the qualification for acquisition of citizenship of Bangladesh on the commencement of the Order by only two categories of persons. In the first category the person must have the three qualifications namely-(i) who or whose father or grandfather was born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh; (ii) who was a permanent resident of such territory on the 25th day of March, 1971 and (iii) who continues to be so resident. For the second category of person the three qualifications are (i) who was a permanent resident of the territory now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971, (ii) who continues to be so resident and (iii) who is not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law for the time being in force. The proviso made provision only for the person who or whose dependent in course of his employment or for the pursuit of his studies was residing in country at war with Bangladesh i.e. in Pakistan and who was prevented from returning to Bangladesh. 

 22. In support of his contention that the petitioner acquired citizenship of Bangladesh by operation of law i.e. PO 149 of 1972 the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to the case of Bishal Deo Tewari Vs. State reported in 27 DLR 622 in particular to the following observation: 

 That case arose out of an order passed by the Deputy Inspector General of Police, Special Branch, Bangladesh and Civil Authority directing Bishal Deo Tewari to reside within the jurisdiction of Sutrapur Police Station under the provisions of Foreigners Order, 1951 and he moved the High Court Division against the order of his detention within the jurisdiction of Lalbagh Police Station by an application under section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure stating, inter-alia that he was a national of Bangladesh having been born in Dhaka and after his studies he was managing and performing Puja of Dhakeswari Mondir as Sebayet. In that view on the facts the High Court Division made the observation quoted above. Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate, submitted that the High Court Division has laid down that a person who was born in Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 continues to be a citizen of Bangladesh, and since the petitioner was born in Bangladesh and he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 he continues to be a citizen of Bangladesh. At first sight, it may appear so if we read the observation quoted above without considering the facts and circumstances under which that case arose. That decision is based on the fact that Bishal Deo Tewari "has been living in this country for generations being born at 23/1 Dhakeswari Road within the Police Station of Lalbagh in the District of Dhaka on 4.10.28. He passed Matriculation Examination from Nabakumar Institution, Dhaka in the year 1948 althrough but he did not prosecute further study and started managing and performing Puja as his parent was shebayet of Dhakeswari Deity. So in that case there was no dispute that being born on 4.10.28 he has been continuously living in this country. So the question of his being continuing permanent resident was not disputed in that case; that is why their Lordships determined his citizenship only on the point as to whether on the 25th March, 1971 he was a resident of Bangladesh. In other words since his birth and his continuous residence in Bangladesh was not questioned, the only point for determination was whether he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971 and finding that he was so resident on the 25th of March, 1971 their Lordships held that he continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh as he was never absent from the territory now comprised in Bangladesh. In my view that decision is of no help in determining the question of acquisition of citizenship by the petitioner in the present case. 

 "The contention of the respondents that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury was a citizen of Pakistan is based upon firstly, that he was away from Bangladesh and then by a notification dated 18.4.73 the Government declared that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury did not qualify to be a citizen of Bangladesh. Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury claimed that he never became a citizen of any other state and his citizenship by statutory provision continued to be Bangladeshi. It appears to us on a perusal of the notification dated 18.4.73 that prior to the said notification Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury by statutory provisions was a citizen of Bangladesh. This notification, however, was subsequently declared void by another notification of the Government dated 19.7.1977. In this view we hold that Mr. Hamidul Huq Chowdhury continued to be a citizen of Bangladesh though he was away from the country." 

 26. The next case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Abdul Hoque Vs. Govt. of Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR 113 and the same case decided by the Appellate Division and reported as the People's Republic of Bangladesh Vs. Abdul Hoque reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 143. In that case Abdul Hoque was admittedly born in Satkhira within Bangladesh in 1932. He was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971; he resided in the then East Pakistan althrough upto November, 1971 when he had to go to the then West Pakistan and he came back to Bangladesh after the political change in August, 1975. He came to Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and on his arrival he surrendered the passport and applied for citizenship of Bangladesh; but the Government refused to grant the same and he was asked to leave the country. So he moved this Court by a Writ Petition and their Lordships of the High Court Division on consideration of the facts and circumstances of that case held him to be a Stateless subject who had no nationality. It was held that he cannot be asked to leave the country. On appeal by the Government, their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that High Court Division was not correct in holding that Abdul Hoque was a Stateless person. Their Lordships noticed the factual position of the case. It was not disputed by the Government that Abdul Hoque was born in this country; that he was a permanent resident of Bangladesh on the 25th March, 1971, that he went to the then West Pakistan on a business tour; that he was an indoor patient in a hospital of Karachi for about 8 months and when he came out from hospital the repatriation process ceased. Thus he returned to Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and surrendered the passport to the Bangladesh Authority; and he applied for citizenship certificate from the Bangladesh Government. The Government having denied the citizenship certificate he filed the writ petition. Their Lordships considered the proviso to Article 2 of PO 149 of 1972 in particular the provision considering the facts of that case held that his temporary absence was covered by the proviso to Article 2 and in the eye of law he remained a resident of Bangladesh. As has been pointed out earlier, the proviso applies to only those categories of persons who in course of his employment or whose dependent for pursuit of his studies was residing in Pakistan and who was prevented from returning to Bangladesh. As a matter of fact Abdul Hoque was a Pan (betel leaf) dealer who used to supply Pan to different dealers in the then West Pakistan and he went to Karachi for collection of his dues. As such their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that his case was covered by the proviso to Article 2. 

 29. In this connection it may be mentioned that citizenship is distinct from nationality and their Lordships of the Appellate Division held in the case of Mirza Shahab Ispahani that citizenship is a creature solely of domestic law. It refers to rights which a state confers upon its national. Mention may be made in this connection to the following observations made by the Supreme Court of India in the case of State Trading Corporation of India Vs. The Commercial Tax Officer reported in AIR 1963 (SC) JB. 

 "But the question still remains whether "nationality" and "citizenship" are interchangeable terms. "Nationality" has reference to the jural relationship which may arise for consideration under international law. On the other hand, "citizenship" has reference to the jural relationship under municipal law. In other words, nationality determines the civil rights of a person, natural or artificial, particularly with reference to international law, whereas citizenship is intimately connected with civil rights under municipal law. Hence all citizens are nationals of a particular State but all nationals may not be citizens of the State. In other words citizens are those persons who have full political rights as distinguished from nationals who may not enjoy full political rights and are still domiciled in that country." 

 30. The learned Advocate in this connection has referred to Chapter 7 of Dicey and Morris on the Conflict of Laws, Eleventh Edition, in particular to Rule 10 at page 128 wherein it is stated that every independent person can acquire domicile of choice by the combination of residence and intention of permanent or indefinite residence but not otherwise; and the learned Advocate has submitted that intention is one of the factors for determination of the citizenship of a person. It may be pointed out that the concepts of domicile or of nationality are matters relating to private international law by which personal rights such as marriage, divorce, majority or minority, the right of succession, etc. are determined and these are different from the rights of citizenship. 

 Relying on this passage the learned Advocate for the petitioner has contended that although Article 3 of the PO 149 of 1972 has been expressly made retrospective in operation from 26.3.1971 but the order contained in the impugned notification dated 18.4.73 cannot act retrospectively. In support of his contention Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate has referred to five cases of the Indian jurisdiction. The first of which is the case of Modi Food Products Ltd. Vs. The Commissioner of Sales Tax reported in AIR 1956 (All.) 35 wherein a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court held that a legislature can certainly give retrospective effect to a piece of legislation passed by it but an executive Government exercising subordinate and delegated legislative powers cannot make legislation retrospective in effect unless that power is expressly conferred by the statute. In that case the petitioner was a dealer in non-edible oils. The UP Sales Tax Act came into force with effect from 1.4.48. The petitioner submitted its return for the period from 6.1.1946 to 3.5.1947. There was an amendment of the UP Sales Tax Act by Act No. XXV of 1948 inserting Section 3A by which a higher rate of Sales Tax was authorised and in exercise of the power under the new section 3A the State Government issued notification on 8.6.48 declaring that with effect from 9.4.48 sales tax shall be at the higher rate. It was in that circumstances held that new amendment will not operate retrospectively. Needless to mention that as a general rule taxing statute does not operate retrospectively. The second case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of ML Bagga-Vs. C Murhar Rao reported in AIR 1956 Hyderabad 35 wherein it has been laid down by a Division Bench that parties were governed by the law in force on the date when a suit is instituted or a proceeding commenced and any subsequent amendment or alteration cannot affect pending proceedings, must always be read subject to the corollary that a legislature could always expressly provide that pending proceeding be affected by an amendment of the law. In that case the respondent moved the Rent Controller on 10.1.55 for an order of eviction of the tenant on the ground of his being a defaulter and an order for eviction was passed but the petitioner claimed protection under a new rule which came into force subsequently and it was held therein that the subsequent new rules have no retrospective effect to protect the tenant from eviction. A similar question came up for consideration before the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Sayedur Rahman Vs. The Chief Election Commissioner, reported in 17 DLR. (SC) 23. In that case Mr. Sayedur Rahman was elected a Member to the Provincial Assembly but he was unseated by the Election Tribunal because of Section 116 of the Representation of People Act, 1957 (Act XXXI of 1957) which provided that a Government Contractor was disqualified to be elected as a Member of the Provincial Assembly. The Dhaka High Court on appeal affirmed the decision of the Election Tribunal. He thereafter filed an appeal before the Supreme Court of Pakistan and during the pendency of the appeal before the Supreme Court the Representation of People Act 1957 was repealed with retrospective effect stating that the Act to be deemed to be repealed on 23rd March, 1962; and as the election was held in May 1962 and the Election Tribunal passed its order on the 7th of February, 1963 the Supreme Court of Pakistan therefore held that there was no doubt that the amending Act was retrospective in operation and since the disqualification was removed by the amending Act, the membership of Mr. Sayedur Rahman was upheld by the Supreme Court. The 3rd case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of Sarder and others Vs. The State reported in AIR 1961 Calcutta 181. In that case an FIR was lodged on 17.12.57 alleging abduction against the accused and charge sheet was submitted on 24.4.58. What happened in that case was that the investigation was started and major portion was completed under the Calcutta Police Act and then by an amendment section 156 of the Cr PC was made applicable by a notification dated 24.2.58. In those circumstances it was held that the subsequent amendment will be of no help for the prosecution. The 4th case referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that of Callcuta Wynad Motor Service (Private) Ltd. Vs. The Stat, of Kera/(l and others reported in AIR 1959 (Kera) 347. In that case what happened is that the term of Regional Transport Authority expired before the order was made on 13.11.58 giving licence for plying of buses in a certain route and the Government by a subsequent notification dated 23.12.58 ordered the continuation of the old Regional Transport Authority and as such it was held that when the executive Government acts as a delegate of a legislative body it had no plenary power to provide for retrospective operation unless and until that power is expressly conferred by the parent enactment and this case was decided following the case report in AIR 1956 (Hyderabad) 35 as referred to above. The next case in this connection referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is the case of India Sugars and Refineries Ltd. Vs. State of Mysore and others reported in AIR 1960 (Mysore) 326 wherein it was held that the power conferred on the Government under the Madras Sugar Factory Control Act, 1949 to levy did not include a power to impose such retrospectively. In that case by certain notification enhanced rate of sales tax was levied. In that case it was held that unless expressly provided, the power to levy can be exercised only prospectively and not retrospectively. 

 34. Another contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner in this connection was that the action of the Government was out and out malafide and the impugned notification was made on account of political enmity and as such the impugned notification was bad in law. It is stated in the petition that Jamaat-e-Islami contested the general election held in 1970 against the Awami League and as such the Awami League Government which was formed after the liberation of Bangladesh was inimical towards the petitioner because of which the impugned notification was made for collateral purpose. But the impugned notification (Annexure-B) itself shows that there are as many as 38 other persons who have also been declared to be deemed not to be citizens of Bangladesh along with the petitioner by the same notification. There is nothing to show that the other 38 belonged to Jamaat-e-Islami. Apparently those persons belonged to different political party and some of them belonged to no political party. Furthermore, before the impugned notification the first general election was held in independent Bangladesh in the month of March, 1973. As such this cannot be treated as a ground for issuance of the impugned notification. I, therefore, hold that there was no malafide in issuing the impugned notification. 

 35. Another point has been raised in this connection by Mr. AR Yusuf, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, as to how a doubt as to the citizenship is to be resolved and the learned Advocate has referred to section 19 of the Citizenship Act, 1951 and Rule 24 of the Citizenship Rule 1952. It may be mentioned here that the learned Attorney-General has laid much stress on the fact that the petitioner on arriving Bangladesh got himself registered as a foreigner and argued that this clearly indicated that he did not treat himself as a citizen of Bangladesh. It may be pointed out that anybody entering into a country with a passport not issued by that country is required to be registered as a foreigner and this is a matter of course only. This in no way could be termed as renunciation of Bangladesh Citizenship. It is not disputed that the petition filed on 8.11.78 for restoration of citizenship of the petitioner has not yet been finally disposed of by the government, or at least, he has not been informed anything in this regard. On the other hand, there are documents attached to the writ petition showing that none else but the Minister-in-charge of the Ministry of Home Affairs in reply to the questions of members, stated in the House of the Nation, that is, the Parliament that the petition of Prof. Golam Azam was under consideration of the government. The last statement in this regard was made on 12.1.92 while the previous statement was made as early as in 1980. From all these facts and circumstance it becomes crystal clear that Prof. Golam Azam never renounced his citizenship of Bangladesh which he acquired by birth and by operation of law. A person cannot be deprived of the citizenship of his country of birth unless be himself renounces it by taking up citizenship of another country in contravention of the law of his country of origin. 

 I am in respectful agreement with the above quoted observations of their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan and hold that the principle of audi alteram partem is not of universal applicability and the question whether this principle should be applied or not depends upon the nature of the thing to be done, the manner in which it is to be done and the circumstances in which it is to be done. The learned Attorney-General has conceded that the principle of natural justice should be followed as far as practicable whenever any person's right is going to be adversely affected by any action whether by a Court of law or a Tribunal or an Administrative Authority. At the same time, he contended that in the present case this doctrine is not at all applicable in view of the fact that the government by the impugned order did not cancel the citizenship of the petitioner nor deprive him of his citizenship. The government in exercise of the power conferred by Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 has given a decision only to remove a doubt as to whether the petitioner fulfilled the requirements of Article 2 so as to be treated as a citizen of Bangladesh or not. His second contention is that since the petitioner was not available in the country and his whereabouts were not known to the Government it was impracticable to serve a show cause notice upon him so as to give him an opportunity of being heard. Whatever may be the language of Article 3 of PO 149 of 1972 there is no doubt about the fact that an order passed under this Article declaring a person not qualified to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh in actual effect interferes with his political status which entails some fundamental rights enumerated in the Constitution which are available to a citizen only. Therefore, it is not worthy to say that by the impugned order no right vested in the petitioner was taken away. Next comes the question whether it was practicable to serve a show cause notice upon the petitioner and the other thirty-eight persons to give them chance to defend themselves as against the proposed action. There is no doubt of the fact that the present petitioner at the relevant time was not available in Bangladesh and therefore, it was not physically possible to serve any notice upon him in person. But our laws provide different modes of service, such as service at the last known residence of the person concerned or by publication in official gazette or in some newspapers and these are treated to be valid and legal service of notice. The government could easily publish a show cause notice either in the gazette or in any newspaper or serve the same at the last known residence in Bangladesh of the petitioner. But this has not been done. This is not a case of emergency as it was in the case of Sayed Abul Ala Moududi. A delay of a month or two in taking a decision regarding the political status of the petitioner and the others mentioned in the notification and to cause service of notice in the meantime would not harm anybody or the public interest or the State of Bangladesh. I am, therefore, of opinion that this is not an exceptional case as has been stated by their Lordships Mr. Fazle Akbar and Mr. Hamoodur Rahman JJ and this being an ordinary case without demanding urgent action, a notice should have been issued asking the person concerned to show cause as to why they should not be declared to be not qualified to be citizens of Bangladesh. Failure to do so has rendered the impugned notification repugnant to the principle of natural justice that no one should be condemned unheard. 

 In the instant case no doubt the impugned order disqualifying the petitioner from being deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh was passed as early as in 1973 and the present writ petition has been filed in March, 1992. So there is a gap of about 19 years. However, the contention of Mr. AR Yusuf is that though the order was issued as early as in 1973 yet no right was threatened till the show cause notice dated 23.3.92 was served upon the petitioner. It is apparent from the writ petition and the other papers that the impugned order, Annexure-B was passed when the petitioner was outside the country. He, after learning about it, had been submitting representation after representation to the executive government for redress of his grievance. Two of his petitions were rejected in 1978 but he was granted visa to visit Bangladesh with a Pakistani passport and immediately after his arrival he surrendered his passport and applied for citizenship on 7.11.78. After lapse of his renewed visa he was not disturbed so far as his stay in Bangladesh was concerned. Rather on 28.1.81 he was asked by the appropriate authority to furnish an affidavit of allegiance which he did the following day. Then there was no reply to his petition. But the Minister-in-charge of the Ministry concerned i.e. the Ministry of Home Affairs, once on 27th May, 1980 and again on 12th January, 1992 made statement in the Parliament to the effect that Prof. Golam Azam's petition for restoration of citizenship was under active consideration of the government. In the meantime, the petitioner was enrolled as voter in the electoral rolls finally published once in 1983 and again in 1990. No doubt the inclusion of the name of the petitioner in the voter list cannot be deemed to have rescinded the Government's Order contained in the impugned notification, Annexure-B dated 18.4.73. But all these facts and circumstances including the inclusion of his name as a voter, Minister's statements in Parliament and top political leaders meeting the petitioner and discussing matters of national importance with him, were sufficient to make the petitioner believe that his petition for restoration of his citizenship was not only under active consideration but under favourable consideration of the Government. Therefore his right to stay in Bangladesh and to exercise the right of franchise an exclusive right of citizens only was not threatened till the notice dated 23.3.92 asking him to show cause why he should not be deported from Bangladesh being a foreigner. Immediately on receipt of this notice the petitioner gave his reply and he being taken into detention moved this Court in its extraordinary original jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. It should be kept in mind that the Supreme Court has always deprecated the tendency to rush to Court before exhausting available administrative remedies. Under the facts and circumstances of this case I am of the opinion that the present writ petition does not suffer from inordinate delay and that the delay that has occurred has been satisfactorily explained.

The court considered that A. Hoque asserted that he was "prevented" from returning to Bangladesh but the circumstances as mentioned by him in the petition namely that he was in hospital for some time and he was prevented from returning to Bangladesh had not been challenged, The' finding of the Appellate Division is that Abdul Hoque remained a resident of Bangladesh and therefore, the court held that the order of deportation must be declared as not lawfully made and the Government appeal was dismissed.

On an examination of the above 3 decided cases on this qualification clause as under Article Z of the Order including the proviso to Art. 2 it thus, appears that the expression permanent resident as occurred in Article 2 has been distinguished from the expression ordinary resident giving permanent resident the status of domicile as it is understood in International Law when it concerns sovereign State. Their Lordships had also, while examining the proviso to Art. 2 which speaks of a prevention clause, in Abdul Hoque's case extended' the sway of the proviso to all that were resident in Pakistan irrespective of being a student or employed as service holder and is being prevented from returning to Bangladesh and this extension of entry to all Bangalees that were "stranded" in Pakistan is found in the Tripartite Agreement signed on 9th of April, 1971 by the Foreign Ministers of India., Pakistan and Bangladesh which agreement was shown to me by the Attorney-General. Governments of these three countries were gratified that such a large number of persons (in their language) "detained and stranded" in these three countries reached their destination which expression 'stranded" is much wider in term and goes beyond persons prevented.

This agreement also brings home the point as I have stated hereinbefore that residence in Pakistan for all the Bangalees by a deeming clause as in Article 2 was considered to be residence in Bangladesh and if one considers 25th March, 1971 to be the starting point then till repatriation started in September, 1973 residence in Pakistan for the period of 30 months till repatriation, would be residence in Bangladesh but in the instant case after 11 months of residence in Pakistan the petitioner was disqualified. 

 120.  In the instant case the petitioner was been here and thus, comes under Article 2(i). He stayed in Bangladesh as permanent resident on 25th of March, 1971 and was present here physically on 25th of March and 26th March, 1971 and he continued to be so permanently resident after the commencing day of the Order and the petitioner is not proved to have gone to Pakistan any time after November, 1972 when he left to reside there permanently. He stayed in Pakistan for 11 months and he stated that his stay in Pakistan was against his will. He went to Lahore" on 22.11.71 temporarily to attend his party meeting while his wife, seven children, father and mother all were living at Dhaka (para-14). After 10 days war broke out on 3.12.71 and he started for Dhaka on the same day by aeroplane but the aeroplane carrying him, after reaching near Dhaka could not land at Dhaka Airport because of war. He was taken back to land at Colombo. Thereafter as there was bombing at Karachi Airport, his plane took him along with others to Jeddah, where after they were taken to Karachi. He had to remain in Karachi against his will for 11 months as the then Government of Pakistan did not allow any Bangladeshi to leave Pakistan and while he was unwillingly staying in Pakistan he in the month of March, 1972 tried to go to London but could not get any passport for that but only for Hajj. He obtained a Pakistani passport as travel document and this was done before repatriation had started for Bangladeshi nationals in September, 1973 and when in Mecca he heard that political mispropaganda is high in Bangladesh against him and he was informed that is his life will be at stake if he went back to Bangladesh. (paras 16, 17, 18). There was no Bangladeshi Embassy in Saudi Arabia also then so he went to London in 1st week of April, 1973 when some days thereafter he was disqualified (Para-19). 

 121.  To all these except a general denial by the State and asserting that he was staying there willingly there is nothing to make those statements improbable. He could have fear of life which fear is rather personal to him as all fears are. He wanted to come back to Bangladesh but he failed. He lived there unwillingly. He was prevented out of fear to return at that time as the political position of the petitioner was then debated and is still been debated. All these do not appear to be unfounded. It was possible for him in that situation to react as he did. I thus, agree with BI Choudhury, J in finding that the petitioner also came under the proviso to Article 2 for his temporary unwilling residence in Pakistan and on the day the impugned notification was issued he was a citizen of Bangladesh by and under the statutory provision as in Article 2. 

 122.  One conduct of the petitioner seems to be clear and it is that after he went out of Pakistan in November, 1972 where he was for some time, he never went back to Pakistan thereafter to seek its nationality or establish a permanent home there. Even in a moment of crisis when he was without the citizenship of Bangladesh and almost a stateless person he did not go to Pakistan or opted for Pakistan which he could do, as many other disqualified persons did. This conduct and this intention to be identified as a Bangladeshi is relevant for the purpose of distinguishing mere residence from domicile of origin. 

 123.  Abdul Hoque's case as referred to hereinbefore covers the point of being prevented from returning but a similar point of being prevented out of political difference of opinion with the then party in power and fear of safety which is also the petitioner's -case is covered by the decision of this court in Hamidul Huq Choudhury's case reported in 33 DLR. It was stated in his writ petition that the then party in power had political hostility and bias against the petitioner, He was a permanent resident but did not return to Bangladesh because of law and order situation and "threat to his life". The Division Bench, in the relevant portion of the judgment (para-15) observed-thus: 

 "The contention of the respondent that Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury was a citizen of Pakistan was based upon firstly, that he was away from Bangladesh and that by notification dated 18A.1973 the Government declared that Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury did not qualify to be a citizen of Bangladesh, Mr. Chowdhury claimed that he never became a citizen of any other state and his citizenship by statutory provision continued to be Bangladeshi. It appears to us on a perusal of notification dated 18.4.73 that prior to the said notification Mr. Hamidul Huq Choudhury by statutory provision was a citizen of Bangladesh. 

 "Relying upon the word "conduct" the learned Attorney-General tried to argue pointing out to certain subsequent events as anti-state activities of the petitioner disentitling him to be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh. But the events and the alleged conduct of the petitioner referred to by the learned Attorney-General may be taken into consideration if any case is made out under Article 2B of the said Presidential Order. Mr. AR Yusuf has pointed out, and in my opinion rightly, that Article 2A and 2B were inserted in PO 149 of 1972 subsequent to the making of the impugned notification the fact remains that the impugned notification was made before the passing of the amending Act or Ordinance. As such, I am of the view that Article 2B 'is not applicable in the present case as the impugned notification was made prior to the insertion of Article 2B in the PO 149 of 1972." 

 129. The learned Attorney-General before me however again laid much emphasis on this "conduct" of the petitioner urging that much papers could not be shown before the Division Bench and with the leave of the court he showed some other writing from the book written by Professor Abu Syeed on the activities of the petitioner subsequent to the independence of Bangladesh in foreign countries. By referring to the book of Prof. Abu Syeed the learned Attorney-General submitted that the petitioner had been in Saudi Arabia after Hajj in a "Politico Military Mission" urging the Muslim countries such as Saudi Arabia and Libya not to recognise Bangladesh and the learned Attorney-General also showed a book published by the petitioner's own party, namely Jamaat-e-Islami, showing that the said Jamat book also corroborated the fact that he was in other Muslim countries like Libya. But while reading the Jamaat book it shows that the petitioner went to those and urged the Muslim countries to help the new State of Bangladesh and that he even obtained money from them through Rabita-e-al- Islami to help the new State of Bangladesh. Which of these versions are true cannot be decided in this writ jurisdiction without knowing the sources of their respective information which source, according to the Attorney-General, are hearsay and they thus being not relevant also, need not be gone into. 

 In the case of Ram Chandra Sankar Deodhar Vs. The State of Maharashtra, a similar point came for consideration before the Supreme Court of India, reported in 1974 SCC at page 317. In that case under report the petitioner challenged the legality of splitting up of the State cadre of Mamlatdars to the Divisional Cadre but moved the writ petition after 12 years of delay. Bhagawati, J who delivered the judgment for the Supreme Court, in meeting this preliminary point of delay, raised by the State, observed thus: 

 148. In the instant case the question is whether the petitioner had explained the delay and moved the court in time when his position was actually threatened in the light of decisions as above. It had been stated by the learned Counsel that when Golam Azam left this country in November, 1971 there was no requirement of a passport to travel between East and West. He went to Lahore in November, 1971 when few days thereafter war broke out between India and Pakistan. Pakistan Army thereafter surrendered. Pakistan did not recognize Bangladesh for some time and the petitioner could not get a travel document from Pakistan to come out of that country or to travel to Bangladesh and then repatriation had not started. So out of necessity he had to obtain a Pakistani passport and with that document he went to Saudi Arabia in November, 1972 only for Hajj and thereafter he went to London in April, 1973 when few days thereafter he was disqualified from being a citizen of Bangladesh. He was not able to come back to Bangladesh because of this political rivalry with the party in power. He had fear of his life and therefore was prevented from coming to Bangladesh. During those days, according to him, he would not get any redress even if he would apply. Thereafter there was change of government in 1975 and in the year 1976 he was again faced with a Notification dated 17.l.76 (Annexure-D) issued by the then Government of Bangladesh asking those persons whose citizenship have been previously" cancelled" to apply for it. He applied for it. There was no reply. A reminder (Annexure-D 1) dated 12.l.77 was sent by him from London and he got a reply (Annexure-E) dated 23.4.77 in which his application was not accepted which he received in London. During those days there was Martial Law in the country and also a state of Emergency proclaimed much earlier on 28th of December, 1974 and because of which emergency fundamental rights as in Arts. 27, 31, 32, 33, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39,40 and 42 were suspended by that emergency, proclaimed by President Mohammadullah and this proclamation of emergency continued throughout the successive governments till it was withdrawn by another proclamation on 27th November, 1979. 

 150. I have given my anxious consideration to the submissions made by the petitioner's lawyer before this court and find that the petitioner's application did not suffer from any sheer negligence to assert a right no' he was indolent or callous. He was hoping to get it and his right was re-offered by Government again in 1974 after he was disqualified in 1973 when things in Bangladesh was against him and fundamental rights suspended. He applied twice, his matter was in the process of being considered on either way as stated in Parliament Leaders in power met him for his party's support, his name appeared in voters list. He was here for long hoping to get registration when he was served with the deportation notice and immediately he came to the Court. In the process no right had accrued to a third party and if his application is heard no prejudice would be caused to the right of any innocent third party. I agree with BJ Chowdhury J when he held that this petition is not so delayed as to be not maintainable.
